text:

text:
Twenty years earlier, Jacob had cheated his twin brother Esau twice: first buying his birthright for a bowl of stew, then tricking their blind father Isaac into giving him the blessing meant for Esau. Esau swore he would kill him, and Jacob fled to his uncle Laban in Haran.

text:

text:

text:

date: ancient Israelite tradition, set c. 1000 BC
text:
The armies of Israel and the Philistines faced each other across the valley of Elah. Every morning and evening for forty days, a Philistine champion named Goliath came out and challenged Israel to send a man to fight him in single combat. He was a giant, armored in bronze from head to foot, with a spear whose shaft was like a weaver's beam. No Israelite dared face him.

text:

text:

text:

text:
After twenty years away, ten at the war in Troy and ten more wandering, Odysseus came home disguised as a beggar, killed the suitors who had been taking over his house, and revealed himself. But his wife Penelope did not run to him. She sat across the hall, looking at him in silence. Their son Telemachus scolded her for her hard heart. text:
Duke Mu of Qin ruled in the 7th century BC in what is now western China. According to the Lushi Chunqiu, compiled in the 3rd century BC, one day some of his fine horses broke loose and wandered off. Local country people at the foot of Mount Qi caught them and ate them, about three hundred men in all.

text:
Thales of Miletus, often called the first Greek philosopher, lived in the 6th century BC. Aristotle, in his Politics, tells a story about him that was already old in Aristotle's time.

People mocked Thales for his poverty, saying it proved that philosophy was useless. text:
A man who wanted to buy a donkey went to the market and found one he liked. Before paying, he asked the seller whether he could take the animal home for a short trial, and the seller agreed.

At home the man led the new donkey into his yard, where his own donkeys were standing, and let it go to see what it would do. The newcomer looked around at all of them. text:
A shepherd boy watched the village sheep on a hillside not far from the houses. The days were long and dull, and one afternoon, to amuse himself, he ran toward the village shouting, "Wolf! Wolf! A wolf is after the sheep!"

text:
In a dry season a crow was nearly dying of thirst. Flying over the fields, she spotted a pitcher standing on the ground and swooped down to it, hoping for water.

There was water inside, but only a little, lying at the very bottom. The neck of the pitcher was narrow and the water was low, and however far she pushed her head in and stretched her beak, she could not reach it. She tried to tip the pitcher over, but it was too heavy for her to move.

text:
A farmer who knew he was dying worried about his sons. They were idle young men, and he feared that once he was gone they would let the farm go to ruin.

He called them to his bedside. "My sons," he said, "I am about to leave this world. Everything I have to give you is in the vineyard. Search there and you will find it." Then he died without saying more.

text:
Four oxen grazed together in the same field. A lion had watched them for a long time and wanted very much to eat them, but whenever he crept close, the oxen turned their tails together and faced outward, so that from every side he met a row of horns. text:
A fox and a stork were on friendly terms, and one day the fox invited the stork to dinner. As a joke, he served the meal as a thin soup poured into a wide, shallow dish. The fox lapped it up easily. The stork, with her long narrow beak, could only wet the tip of it and went home as hungry as she had come. The fox said he was sorry she had not enjoyed the soup.

text:
A flock of pigeons lived in fear of a kite. Every so often it swooped on the dovecote and carried one of them off, and the pigeons could find no way to stop it.

At last they had an idea. The hawk was stronger than the kite and could drive it away. They went to the hawk and asked him to be their defender. He agreed at once, with every appearance of goodwill, and they opened the dovecote and invited him in.

text:
A lark built her nest in a field of young wheat in early spring. By summer her chicks were nearly ready to fly, and the wheat around them had ripened.

One day the farmer came with his son to look at the crop. It was time to harvest, he said; he would ask his neighbors to come and help reap it. text:

text:
In spring a swallow saw a farmer sowing seed in a field and recognized it: hemp, or in some versions flax. She gathered the other birds and warned them. That seed, she said, would grow into the plant men twist into cord and weave into the nets they use to catch birds. Now, while it lay on the ground, they should pick up every grain and eat it.

text:
In the middle of a battle, a trumpeter who had been sounding the charge and urging his side forward was cut off and captured by the enemy.

He pleaded for his life. He told his captors that he had done them no harm at all. He had not killed a single one of their men. He carried no sword or spear, nothing but his brass trumpet, so it would be unjust to put him to death.

text:

text:
Confucius was traveling past the side of Mount Tai with some of his disciples when he came upon a woman weeping bitterly beside a grave. He listened to her for a while, then sent his disciple Zilu to ask what had happened.

Zilu said to her that she wept like someone who had suffered sorrow upon sorrow. She told him it was so. Some years ago her husband's father had been killed by a tiger in this place. Then her husband had been killed by a tiger. And now her son had died the same way.

text:
Once the parts of the body held a meeting and made a complaint. The hands worked from morning to night, the feet walked everywhere, the mouth chewed and the teeth ground, and all of it went to the belly, which lay at the center doing nothing but receiving. text:

text:

Themistocles of Athens believed the only chance was to fight in the narrow strait, where the larger Persian fleet could not use its numbers. He was losing the argument.

location: Rome and the Alban Hills (modern Italy)
text:
In 458 BC, according to the Roman historian Livy, a Roman army under the consul Minucius was trapped by the Aequi in a mountain valley. The Senate decided the city needed a dictator, a temporary ruler with near-absolute power, and chose Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus, a former consul who was then working a small farm of about four acres across the Tiber.

text:
Kisa Gotami was a young woman of Savatthi whose only son died when he was just old enough to run about. Unable to accept it, she carried the small body on her hip from house to house, asking everyone for medicine that would cure him. People thought she had lost her mind.

title: Creon and Antigone
text:
After the brothers Eteocles and Polynices killed each other in a war for the throne of Thebes, their uncle Creon became king. He decreed that Eteocles, who had defended the city, would be buried with honor, while Polynices, who had attacked it, would be left unburied for the dogs and birds. Anyone who buried him would die.

Their sister Antigone defied him. She covered her brother's body with dust and performed the rites, declaring that the unwritten laws of the gods outranked any king's decree.

location: From Cunaxa (modern Iraq) to Trapezus (modern Trabzon, Turkey)
text:
In 401 BC more than ten thousand Greek mercenaries marched deep into the Persian Empire for Cyrus the Younger, who was trying to overthrow his brother, King Artaxerxes. At Cunaxa, near Babylon, the Greeks won their part of the battle, but Cyrus was killed. They were stranded in the heart of a hostile empire, far from the sea.

text:

Karna grew into a great warrior, but because people believed he was a charioteer's son, he was mocked by the princes, and the only one who honored him was Duryodhana. Karna became his loyal friend, and so an enemy of the Pandavas, Kunti's fiv

text:
During their exile in the forest, the five Pandava brothers grew desperately thirsty. Nakula went looking for water and found a clear lake. A voice warned him not to drink until he had answered its questions. He ignored it, drank, and fell dead. Sahadeva, Arjuna and Bhima followed one by one and met the same fate.

location: Yueyang, capital of Qin (modern Shaanxi, China)
text:
In the fourth century BC Shang Yang, a minister serving Duke Xiao of Qin, prepared a sweeping set of new laws meant to make Qin strong: rewards for farming and for military merit, punishments for idleness, and a strict system of mutual responsibility.

text:
Plutarch tells this story in his Life of Alexander. A horse dealer from Thessaly named Philonicus brought a horse called Bucephalus to King Philip of Macedon, asking thirteen talents for him, an enormous price. When they took him out to the field to try him, the horse was wild. He reared up and would not let any of the king's men mount him or even speak to him. They were leading him away as useless.

title: Alexander Drinks the Suspect Medicine
text:
In 333 BC, as Alexander the Great marched through Cilicia toward the Persian king Darius, he fell dangerously ill. Some said he caught a chill bathing in the icy river Cydnus. According to Plutarch, his physicians thought the case so desperate that none dared treat him, fearing the anger of the Macedonians if he died in their care.

text:

text:
King Xuan of Qi asked Mencius whether someone like him could become a true king who protects his people. Mencius said yes, and gave a reason. He had heard that the king, sitting in his hall, once saw an ox being led past. The animal was to be killed so its blood could consecrate a new bell. text:

text:

The Strategies of the Warring States says he kept complaining by singing to his sword about having no fish to eat, no carriage and no means to support his mother, and Lord Mengchang provided each.

text:

text:

text:

text:

The god Vishnu told them that they could regain their power by drinking amrita, the nectar of immortality, which lay hidden at the bottom of the cosmic ocean of milk. text:

text:
In 578, according to the company's records, Prince Shotoku of Japan brought skilled carpenters from the Korean kingdom of Baekje to build Shitenno-ji, a great Buddhist temple in what is now Osaka. One of them, Shigemitsu Kongo, stayed on. His family founded Kongo Gumi, a construction company that went on to build and repair temples for more than fourteen hundred years, longer than any other known company.

The family kept the business alive through wars, fires and the rise and fall of dynasties.

title: Frigg's Oath for Baldr
text:
Baldr, son of Odin and Frigg, was the best loved of all the gods, so fair and bright that light seemed to shine from him. One night he began to have terrible dreams that his life was in danger. When he told the other gods, they decided to protect him.

His mother Frigg traveled through all the worlds and took oaths from everything to do Baldr no harm: fire and water, iron and every metal, stones, earth, trees, sicknesses, beasts, birds, poisons and serpents. Afterward the gods made a game of it.

text:

Most people know the gap between intending to do something and actually doing it. The German psychologist Peter Gollwitzer proposed a simple bridge: an implementation intention, a plan in the form "When situation X arises, I will do Y." location: A manufacturing company in the United States
text:

She combined surveys of team members, interviews and her own observations, and gathered ratings of each team's performance from managers and internal customers.

Her focus was a quality she called psychological safety: a shared belief in the team that it is safe to take interpersonal risks.
